title: Default Address Selection for Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6)
summary: Describes algorithms for choosing a source address and a destination address in IPv6. They give default behavior for all IPv6 implementations, without overriding choices made by applications or upper-layer protocols. This matters when a host has several addresses and a destination has several to try. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: If you have many house keys and a friend has many doors, you need a rule for which key and which door to use. This memo gives the default rules for computers.

questions: how does ipv6 choose a source address
what is the default address selection policy
ipv6 or ipv4 which is preferred by default
what is the ipv6 policy table
how to make a host prefer ipv4 over ipv6
subtitle: How an IPv6 host picks which of its addresses to send from, and which of a peer's addresses to try first.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 node often has several source addresses of different scopes and states, and a DNS name can return several destination addresses, both IPv6 and IPv4. Without common rules, behavior is hard to predict.
tldr.mechanism: Two rule-based algorithms sort the candidates pair by pair: one picks a source address, the other orders destination addresses. They share a policy table that administrators can override.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6724 obsoletes RFC 3484 and sets the default behavior, including a preference for IPv6 over IPv4 when matching source addresses are available.

facts.label: Scope of use
facts.value: All IPv6 nodes, hosts and routers

today: RFC 6724 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3484. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Address Selection Is Needed
sections.content:
IPv6 lets an interface hold several unicast addresses. They can differ in reach (link-local, site-local or global), in state (preferred or deprecated), in purpose (public or temporary) and in role (home address or care-of address in mobility). Multi-homing, tunnels and virtual interfaces add still more addresses.

Dual-stack hosts face a second choice. When DNS returns both IPv6 and IPv4 addresses, a blunt rule such as always prefer IPv6 can go wrong. The RFC's example: with a global IPv6 address and only an auto-configured 169.254/16 IPv4 address, IPv6 is best; with only a link-local IPv6 address and a global IPv4 address, IPv4 is best.

The goal is defaults common to all implementations so developers and administrators can predict behavior. The rules never override an application's or upper layer's explicit choice of a legal source or destination address.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer can have lots of addresses, like a kid with many nicknames. When it talks to someone, it needs a fair rule for which name to use and which of the other person's addresses to call first.

sections.title: Where the Algorithms Run
sections.content:
The RFC assumes the common implementation split. An application calls an API such as getaddrinfo(), gets a list of addresses, and passes one to the network stack with connect() or sendto(). So the network layer never has to choose a destination, but it often has to choose a source, because applications usually leave it unspecified.

That gives two algorithms. The destination algorithm is meant to sort the list that APIs like getaddrinfo() return. The source algorithm is used by the IPv6 network layer when no source was specified. Well-behaved applications SHOULD NOT use only the first address and give up; they should walk the list, or try several in parallel with a small delay.

Responders are covered too. Often a reply just swaps the addresses of the received packet, but a reply to a multicast request still needs source selection. Choosing which local addresses to listen on is out of scope.

The combined effect: prefer pairs of equal scope or type, prefer smaller scope for the destination, prefer non-deprecated sources, avoid transitional addresses when native ones exist, and otherwise prefer the longest common prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: An app asks for a list of places a friend can be reached, then the computer sorts that list from best to worst. Separately, it picks which of its own addresses to put on the envelope.

sections.title: The Policy Table and Address Properties
sections.content:
The policy table is a longest-matching-prefix lookup, like a routing table. For an address A it returns Precedence(A), used to sort destinations, and Label(A), which lets a source prefix be preferred for a destination prefix: a source S is preferred with destination D when Label(S) = Label(D).

Implementations SHOULD allow this to be configured. If not configured, they SHOULD use the default table below. An implementation MAY add site-specific rows automatically (for example for ULAs and 6to4 prefixes), but such rows MUST NOT override a row configured by other means, and there SHOULD be an Automatic Row Additions flag to turn this off.

To compare unlike addresses, Section 3 defines mappings. IPv4 addresses are handled as IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses. IPv4 169.254/16 and 127/8 get link-local scope; other IPv4 addresses, including private and Shared Address Space ones, get global scope, and IPv4 addresses count as preferred. Addresses with embedded IPv4 (IPv4-compatible, IPv4-mapped, IPv4-converted, IPv4-translatable and 6to4) have global scope. The IPv6 loopback address has link-local scope.

The common prefix length CommonPrefixLen(S, D) compares only up to the length of S's prefix, not the interface ID. For example, CommonPrefixLen(fe80::1, fe80::2) is 64.
sections.plainLanguage: The policy table is a scoreboard. Each kind of address gets a score and a team color, and the rules use the scores and colors to settle which address wins.

sections.title: Choosing a Source Address
sections.content:
First the node builds a candidate set. It is RECOMMENDED to use the unicast addresses of the outgoing interface. For multicast and link-local destinations the candidates MUST come from the same link, and multicast and unspecified addresses MUST NOT be candidates. If an application names a source that is not in the candidate set, that is an error; if it is in the set, the choice MUST be respected.

Then rules act as ordered tiebreakers. Only addresses that tie on one rule go on to the next, and if the rules fail to choose one, the final tiebreaker is implementation-specific. The key rules are: prefer the same address as the destination; prefer an appropriate scope; avoid deprecated addresses; prefer home addresses; prefer the outgoing interface; prefer a prefix advertised by the next hop (Rule 5.5, only for implementations that track it); prefer a matching label; prefer temporary addresses; and finally use the longest matching prefix.

Rule 7 is a privacy choice. Applications MUST be able to reverse it per application, and there SHOULD be a Privacy Preference flag. The RFC admits the risk that short-lived temporary addresses can break some applications.
sections.plainLanguage: To pick which return address to write on a letter, you check a list of questions in order, such as which one fits the destination and which is not old. The first question that has a clear winner decides.

sections.title: Ordering Destination Addresses
sections.content:
The destination algorithm sorts a list holding IPv6 and IPv4 addresses together. IPv4 addresses are looked up as IPv4-mapped addresses. Each destination D is paired with Source(D), its selected source, which is undefined if no source is available. Ten rules MUST be applied in order, and the first rule that decides ends the comparison.

The rules avoid unusable destinations, prefer matching scope, avoid deprecated sources, prefer home addresses, prefer matching label, then prefer higher precedence. After that come native transport over encapsulating tunnels (such as 6rd, ISATAP and configured tunnels), smaller scope, longest matching prefix, and finally the original order. Rules 9 and 10 MAY be superseded if the implementation knows better, for example which address gives the best performance.

Because the default table gives IPv6 higher precedence than IPv4, IPv6 wins when matching sources exist. Section 7 notes that routing is assumed to come first, though source considerations MAY break ties between equal routes. Section 8 requires that cached sorted lists be no more than one second out of date.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine sorting a list of ways to reach a friend. You throw out the ones that are broken, then prefer the ones that fit well, and only at the end keep the order you were given.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Notes
sections.content:
The RFC says it has no direct impact on Internet infrastructure security, but it names three concerns.

  • Source selection can leak correlations. An unfriendly node can send requests that force the target to pick a source for its reply, and so learn which addresses belong together. Preferring temporary addresses helps mitigate this.
  • Address selection influences the path taken, and so whether traffic crosses a more or less trusted network. Administrators should weigh the security impact of each policy table row.
  • Administrative options must be secured against illicit modification, or an attacker could redirect or block traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger can make you reveal which nicknames you use, they can tell they are all you. Using short-lived nicknames makes that harder.

sections.title: Worked Examples and Policy Tweaks
sections.content:
Section 10 is illustrative, not normative. It first shows default results, then shows how policy table edits change them.

  • Prefer IPv4: raising the ::ffff:0:0/96 precedence to 100 makes IPv4 sort ahead of IPv6. This also helps with "broken" IPv6, where a host has a global IPv6 address but no real IPv6 connectivity and the default table causes timeouts.
  • Link-local last: adding fe80::/10 with precedence 33 sorts global destinations before link-local ones.
  • Multi-homed site: with the default table, longest matching prefix sends site A's traffic to site B over the normal ISP rather than their high-performance ISP. Rows for 2001:db8:1aaa::/48 and 2001:db8:1bbb::/48 with precedence 43 and label 6 fix this.
  • ULA and 6to4: by default global destinations beat ULA ones, and NATed IPv4 beats 6to4. A site-specific row with precedence 45 and label 14 reverses that for the site's own prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show that if the default rules do not fit your house, you can change the scoreboard, for instance telling every computer to try the older road first.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 3484
sections.content:
Appendix B lists what changed. In the table: rows were added for Teredo (2001::/32), ULAs, site-local addresses and 6bone (3ffe::/16); 6to4 was depreferenced below native IPv4; IPv4-compatible addresses were depreferenced. Optional automatic rows for site-specific ULA and 6to4 prefixes were also added.

In the rules: CommonPrefixLen() now compares only up to the source prefix length, so DNS load balancing can still act as a tiebreaker. Source Rule 5.5 was added to cope with ingress filtering. The ban on anycast source addresses was dropped. RFC 1918 addresses moved from site-local to global scope. Source Rule 7 now defaults to temporary addresses over public ones, with an administrative override.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the list of fixes made since the first version of the rules, like updating a game after players found problems.

items.label: Precedence 40, Label 1
items.desc: Default row for addresses not matched by a longer prefix.

items.label: Precedence 35, Label 4
items.desc: IPv4-mapped addresses, so IPv4 ranks just below native IPv6.

viz.caption: SOURCE ADDRESS SELECTION RULES, IN ORDER

items.label: Prefer same address
items.desc: A candidate equal to the destination wins.

items.label: Prefer appropriate scope
items.desc: Avoid a source with smaller scope than the destination.

items.label: Avoid deprecated addresses
items.desc: A preferred address beats a deprecated one.

items.label: Prefer outgoing interface
items.desc: Use an address on the interface that will send the packet.

items.label: Prefer next-hop prefix
items.desc: Prefer an address from a prefix advertised by the chosen next hop.

viz.caption: DESTINATION ADDRESS ORDERING RULES, IN ORDER

items.label: Avoid unusable destinations
items.desc: Unreachable, or no source address available.

items.label: Prefer matching scope
items.desc: Destination scope equals its source's scope.

items.label: Avoid deprecated addresses
items.desc: Avoid destinations whose source is deprecated.
